notes:
I found no real split between denominations on Ezekiel 23:1–24. The disagreements I did find are between individual commentators, not traditions. The modern-scholarship notes come from Bible Odyssey. I didn't get to NET Bible notes or any Orthodox site. The only Catholic material is Jerome and the Vulgate on v. 23, reported second-hand. I found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings, so those are left out.

## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**Chapter overview**
- **Constable** (bible.org-style notes, on studylight) compares this chapter with ch. 16. He says ch. 16 is mostly about spiritual adultery (idolatry), while ch. 23 is mostly about political adultery: trusting foreign alliances. Ch. 16 deals with Judah alone, while ch. 23 covers both kingdoms but mainly Judah. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-23.html
- Constable also cites Stuart that this is "the most graphic language in the Bible in reference to sexual imagery", so it needs great care in teaching. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-23.html
- **Kingcomments** notes that ch. 16 ends with hope; that hope is missing from this chapter. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/ezekiel-23.html

**v. 1–2**
- **Guzik:** the two sisters stand for the two kingdoms. The picture isn't a perfect match, since the Lord did not have two wives. Its point is that Judah walked in Israel's steps. Quoting Block, he adds that unlike the foundling of ch. 16, these women are not meant to be pitied. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-23/
- **Kingcomments:** "daughters of one mother" indicates that Israel was originally one people. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/ezekiel-23.html
- **Pulpit Commentary:** the story treats the sisters as separate even in Egypt. The commentator thinks this was probably true historically, because tension between Ephraim and the other tribes shows up long before Jeroboam's revolt. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-23.html

**v. 3**
- **Guzik:** Israel was unfaithful from the start, worshipping Egyptian idols. He points to the golden calf, Joshua 24:14 and Jeroboam's calves. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-23/
- **Constable** also cites the golden calf and Joshua 24:14 as evidence of idolatry picked up in Egypt. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-23.html

**v. 4**
- **The names:** Oholah means "her tent" and Oholibah "my tent is in her." Samaria's worship was her own invention, while Jerusalem had God's temple. Sources:
  - Barnes: https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/23-4.html
  - Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/23-4.htm
- **Constable** suggests "her tent" may refer to pagan tent shrines. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-23.html
- **Pulpit:** Jerusalem's privilege made her guilt worse. Proper names almost never appear in Bible parables; the only other case is Lazarus in Luke 16. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-23.html
- **"Elder":** Keil and others read the word as "greater," meaning the northern kingdom's greater power. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/23-4.htm
- **"Sons and daughters":** Constable takes these as the cities' inhabitants and surrounding villages. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-23.html
- **Does the story imply God married two sisters?** Constable warns against pressing the picture that far. Citing Chisholm, he says using the image doesn't mean God approved of bigamy. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-23.html

**v. 5–6**
- **Guzik:** Israel envied Assyria's power and fame and took on its gods and customs. He cites Wiersbe and Taylor on Jehu bowing before Shalmaneser on the Black Obelisk (about 840 BC). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-23/
- **Constable** cites the same obelisk and references in 2 Kings and Hosea. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-23.html
- **Pulpit:** "blue" is the same word used for the tabernacle hangings, probably the official dress of Assyrian officers. The cavalry was a force Israel always lacked. "Neighbors" probably means spiritual closeness, not geography. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-23.html

**v. 7–8**
- **Guzik**, citing Block: the word "all" appears three times in v. 7, showing she held nothing back. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-23/
- **Pulpit:** Samaria probably took up Assyrian worship, perhaps of Ishtar as queen of heaven. Her kings then tried to play Assyria and Egypt off against each other. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-23.html

**v. 9–10**
- **Guzik**, citing Feinberg: the source of sinful pleasure becomes the source of punishment. He ties the verses to Assyria's conquest in 722 BC. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-23/
- **Constable:** she became notorious for her sins, the way the name "Jezebel" still is. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-23.html
- **Pulpit:** "a byword" literally means "a name among women": infamous among the nations. It was Hoshea's double-dealing that led to the siege of Samaria. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-23.html

**v. 11–13**
- **Guzik:** Jerusalem's guilt was greater because she saw Samaria judged and copied her anyway. He cites Ahaz's alliance with Assyria and the altar he copied (2 Kings 16). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-23/
- **Pulpit:** traces the same pattern through Ahaz, Hezekiah, Manasseh and Josiah. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-23.html
- **Matthew Henry:** people who don't learn from God's judgments on others can expect judgment themselves. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_023.cfm

**v. 14–15**
- **Barnes:** the palace walls of Nineveh had exactly such figures, colored with red ochre. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/23-14.htm
- **Keil & Delitzsch:** these were war scenes and processions on Assyrian palace walls, not mythological figures. Judah's contact with this splendor drew her into dealings with Babylon and then its idolatry. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/23-14.htm
- **Gill** reads it differently: the images may have been deified heroes or idols such as Bel or Nebo, painted on temple or house walls and worshipped. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/23-14.htm
- **Cambridge Bible:** the prophet is combining a Babylonian custom with reports reaching Judah; such pictures probably weren't actually seen in Jerusalem. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/23-14.htm
- **Guzik:** "the land of their nativity" may recall that Abraham came out of Chaldea; his descendants were going back to what God called him from. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-23/
- **Pulpit** links the envoys to Merodach-Baladan's embassy (Isaiah 39) and Manasseh's stay in Babylon. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-23.html

**v. 16**
- **Guzik**, quoting Trapp: the trouble started with the eye. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-23/
- **BibleHub study note:** compares Eve seeing the tree (Gen 3:6) and Psalm 101:3. https://biblehub.com/ezekiel/23-14.htm

**v. 17–18**
- **Constable:** after becoming Babylon's vassal, Judah grew disgusted and turned to Egypt; God in turn grew disgusted with her. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-23.html
- **Pulpit** compares Amnon (2 Samuel 13:15), whose lust turned to loathing. It notes Jeremiah advised accepting Babylonian rule. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-23.html

**v. 19–21**
- **Constable:** donkeys and horses were proverbial for strong sexual drive and here picture Egypt's appealing potency. Jerusalem went back to her old lover. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-23.html
- **Guzik:** the idea is that powerful nations could protect Judah. He also links the imagery to sexual rites in pagan worship. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/ezekiel/ezekiel-23.cfm
- **Pulpit:** the word for "paramours" usually means a concubine and is used here in scorn of Egypt's princes. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-23.html
- **Bob Utley (bible.org):** the language is meant to shock and sicken God's people about idolatry, meaning foreign alliances. https://bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-23

**v. 22–23**
- **Matthew Henry:** God often turns what sinners set their hearts on into the whip that punishes them. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_023.cfm
- **Pulpit:** "desirable young men" is repeated sarcastically. Assyrians are included because they now fought in Nebuchadnezzar's armies. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-23.html
- **Pekod, Shoa and Koa** (see section 2 for the debate):
  - Constable takes them as tribes of eastern Babylonia. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-23.html
  - Clarke says no geographer has ever located them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/ezekiel-23.html

**v. 24**
- **Pulpit:** the first word in the list probably means "armor." "According to their judgments" means Babylon would carry out God's sentence in its own cruel way. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-23.html
- **Gill:** they would judge by their own laws, treating Judah as rebels and covenant-breakers. Zedekiah, for example, broke his oath to Babylon. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/23-24.html
- **Matthew Henry:** Babylon had right as well as might on its side. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_023.cfm
- **Coffman:** this points ahead to v. 25. Mutilation was not allowed under God's law but was used in Mesopotamia. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/23-24.html

## 2. Where interpreters differ

- **Idolatry or politics?**
  - Constable sees mainly political alliances. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-23.html
  - Guzik says idolatry was "often connected with" alliances, so it was both. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-23/
  - Coffman, on vv. 19–20, insists on literal sexual sin. He argues no political alliances were possible in Egypt. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/23-20.html

- **v. 23, names or titles?**
  - Clarke (Methodist): proper names, though no one can locate them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/ezekiel-23.html
  - Benson (Methodist): most ancient writers took them as provinces of Babylon. Jerome took them as titles of rank. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/ezekiel-23.html
  - Pulpit: the Vulgate and Luther render "nobles, tyrants, princes," and Keil and Hengstenberg follow that. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-23.html
  - Grotius matched them to specific peoples: Bactrians, a people in Armenia, and Medes. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tcc/ezekiel-23.html
  - Ellicott prefers "rulers, lords, and nobles." https://biblehub.com/ezekiel/23-23.htm
  
  This is a question of translation, not denomination.

- **v. 4:** the Geneva Bible (Reformed) gives the same tent meanings as everyone else. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/23-4.htm

## 3. Other views

- **Modern scholarship (Bible Odyssey):**
  - The chapter portrays Israel's and Judah's alliances with empires as wives chasing powerful foreign men. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/oholah-and-oholibah/
  - The metaphor assumes ancient marriage law, in which wives were not equal and husbands had sexual rights over them. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/oholah-and-oholibah/
  - Some scholars think the violence reflects the trauma of war and exile. Others warn the image carries negative assumptions about women, especially if read literally. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/ezekiel/
  - Some writers try to rescue the marriage metaphor by pointing to its passages about reconciliation. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/marriage-metaphors-in-the-prophets/

- **Catholic (v. 23):** Jerome and the Vulgate read the three names as titles of rank. This comes through Benson and Pulpit; I didn't read Jerome directly. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/ezekiel-23.html
